title: Salutation to the armed One
hook: namo sastr paane: salutation to the One with weapons in hand, the protector (Jaap)
tomorrow: Sun of suns, moon of moons

segments.voice: Yesterday, ajooni, never born, not made of earth or water, and your line, not made of this. Today Jaap does something surprising: after formless and unborn, it puts a weapon in the One's hand.

A lifeguard's whistle. A crossing guard's raised hand and bright vest. A parent stepping, without thinking, between a child and a dog that's barking too hard. Protection doesn't always look gentle. Sometimes it's loud, and fast, and holding something: a rescue tube, a stop sign. The people who stand between us and harm are rarely remembered as soft. They're remembered as there. Jaap Sahib has a line for the One who stands there.
screen: `A LIFEGUARD'S WHISTLE.` → `A PARENT STEPS BETWEEN.` → `PROTECTION ISN'T ALWAYS GENTLE.`

segments.voice: Among the salutations comes namo sastr paane. Namo, a bow. Sastr, or shastar, is a weapon held in the hand, like a sword. Paan is the hand. Salutation to the One with weapons in hand. The next words add astr, a weapon that's thrown or shot, like an arrow: the One honored with that weapon too. Right after aroop and ajooni, it can startle. Why would the formless need a sword? Because for the Tenth Guru, the sword is a picture of protection. He lived in violent years. His father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was executed in Delhi. The Guru himself fought battles to defend his people, and in his Persian letter, the Zafarnama, he speaks of the four sons he lost. In that letter he wrote, in effect, that when every other way has failed, it is right to take up the sword. Not first. Last. So the weapon in the One's hand isn't a threat to the innocent; it's the arm that defends them. The idea runs through Sikh life. The Ardas, the prayer said at the close of Sikh gatherings, begins by remembering Bhagauti, a name for the Divine as sword and power. Amritdhari Sikhs carry the kirpan, a small sword, as an article of faith, a promise to protect, not a tool for picking fights. And the ideal has a name you met last year: sant sipahi, the saint-soldier. Gentle in the heart, ready in the hands. Jaap bows to the One who is both.
screen: `SASTR: A WEAPON HELD IN THE HAND.` · `WHY DOES THE FORMLESS NEED A SWORD?` · `ZAFARNAMA: THE SWORD COMES LAST.` · `SANT SIPAHI: THE SAINT-SOLDIER.` · then, large: `THE PROTECTOR.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who protects you, or once did, a parent, a teacher, a nurse, a stranger who stepped in, and the moment they stood between you and harm. Breathe in and remember what that safety was like; breathe out, thank them silently, and wonder, gently, who you might stand in front of. If you pray, you can say namo sastr paane.
Shastar. A weapon held in the hand — namo sastr paane, Jaap's bow to the One with weapons in hand, the protector who defends the weak.
Your line: the protector. The sword comes last, and it's there to defend. Day three hundred forty-one.

screen: `DAY 341 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SUN OF SUNS, MOON OF MOONS.`

original.note: Gurmukhi: shastar, a weapon held in the hand; Jaap writes it sastr, in namo sastr paane.

trapdoor: what you thought: the armed One sounds like a warlike God.
what it means: the weapon is a picture of protection, the arm that defends the weak, used last, not first.
what a scholar hears: Jaap pairs sastr (hand-held weapon) and astr (missile); the Zafarnama, addressed to Aurangzeb, frames armed resistance as lawful only after all other means fail.
recall: the script of the Guru Granth Sahib

chat.says: Why does a prayer about a formless God mention weapons at all?
options: For the Tenth Guru the sword means protection: the arm that defends the weak, used last.
It's a call to strike first, so enemies learn to fear Sikhs before trouble starts.
The weapons are only decoration from old poems, with no meaning for Sikhs today.
chat.meaning: In Jaap the weapon is a picture of protection; the Zafarnama says the sword is right only when every other way has failed.
